title: Yasya vaikaṅkatī: the ladle of vikaṅkata wood
theme: A single ritual rule: the agnihotra ladle should be of vikaṅkata wood, so that the offerings stand firm, and the offerer with them.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «वैकङ्कती विकङ्कताख्येन वृक्षेण निष्पादिता» — made from the tree called vikaṅkata
The anonymous commentator: «अग्निहोत्रे हविर्हूयते यया दर्व्या सेयमग्निहोत्रहवणी» — the ladle with which the oblation is offered in the agnihotra
The anonymous commentator: «प्रतितिष्ठन्त्येव फलप्रदा भवन्त्येव» — they stand firm, that is, they bear fruit
The anonymous commentator: «अनुष्ठातुश्चित्तशुद्धिद्वारा तत्वज्ञानप्रतिष्ठार्थं संपद्यन्ते» — they serve to establish the performer in knowledge of reality, through purity of mind

sandhi.rule: ī becomes y before another vowel (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)): vaikaṅkatī + agnihotra° → vaikaṅkaty agnihotra°.

sandhi.type: i before a vowel; like vowels merge; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: prati + eva → praty eva (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)); eva + asya and asya + āhutayaḥ merge into long ā (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)): evāsyāhutayaḥ; the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)); tiṣṭhanti + atho → tiṣṭhanty atho.

morphology.note: A derivative meaning ‘made of vikaṅkata’, feminine to agree with havaṇī. Bhāskara explains the suffix by P. 4.3.141 (पलाशादिभ्यो वा), which allows it for the names of certain trees.
The preverb prati stands apart from its verb tiṣṭhanti, as Vedic prose allows (tmesis): prati … tiṣṭhanti, ‘stand firm’. The last word, pratiṣṭhityai, is the noun from the same verb.

translation.literal: He whose agnihotra ladle is made of vikaṅkata — his offerings indeed stand firm; and [it is] for firm standing.
translation.readable: If the ladle with which a man makes the agnihotra offering is made of vikaṅkata wood, his offerings stand firm; and it gives him a firm footing too.

syntax: A relative clause (yasya … bhavati, ‘whose … is’) followed by the main clause in which the preverb prati is separated from its verb tiṣṭhanti by eva asya āhutayaḥ. A last phrase, atho pratiṣṭhityai (‘and for firm standing’), states a further purpose.

ambiguities.note: Whose firm standing? Bhāskara: the sacrificer’s, «तस्यापि यजमानस्य प्रतिष्ठित्यै सा भवति». The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the performer’s establishment in knowledge of reality, reached through a purified mind.

A rule about a ladle sits among hymns and mantras of worship. The commentators explain its place differently: as standing for all Vedic rites as aids to release (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa), or as praise of the god in the form of fire (Bhāskara).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A Brāhmaṇa-style rule in prose, 30 syllables in one line.

beginner: Among the hymns and prayers of this Upaniṣad stands one plain ritual rule. The agnihotra is the daily offering of milk into the sacred fire, poured with a ladle. The rule says: if that ladle is made from the wood of the vikaṅkata tree, the offerings ‘stand firm’, and the one who offers gains a firm footing too. Why is a rule about a ladle here? The old commentators answer in two ways. One says that in a text about release, this tree stands for all the rites of the Veda, which, done rightly, purify the mind and so prepare it for knowledge. Another connects the tree with an old story in which the vikaṅkata grew where the first offering stood firm. The text states the rule; it does not claim any further effect.
analogy: Like a craftsman’s rule about which wood to use for a handle: a small choice that is meant to make the whole work hold.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That for one whose agnihotra ladle is made of vikaṅkata, the offerings stand firm, and it serves for firm standing.

commentary.q: Why does a ritual rule stand in this text?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the rule prescribes a tree for an instrument of the agnihotra, «अग्निहोत्रकर्मणि होमसाधनद्रव्यस्य कारणभूतं वृक्षविशेषं विधत्ते», and the tree stands for all the rites of the Veda as means to release, through purity of mind: «मुमुक्षोश्चित्तशुद्धिद्वारा वेदोक्तानां कृत्स्नकर्मणां मोक्षसाधनत्वं द्योतयितुमुपलक्षणत्वेन कर्माङ्गभूतो विकङ्कतवृक्षो विहितः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara quotes, without naming its source, a passage that the vikaṅkata arose where the first offering stood firm, and from it creatures were made: «सा यत्राहुतिः प्रत्यतिष्ठत्ततो विकङ्कत उदतिष्ठत्ततः प्रजा असृजत». Since the tree is tied to creation, the rule here honours the god who makes the world grow in the form of fire; knowing this, he says, one should worship that god: «एवं ज्ञात्वाऽग्न्यात्मानं देवमाराधयेद् उपासीतेति».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read the rule as standing for all Vedic rites as aids to release; Bhāskara as praise of the god in the form of fire.

contemporary.text: The rule is about a ladle, yet the text places it among its hymns. Whatever one makes of the ritual, the thought that a small, exact choice of means can steady a whole practice is familiar from any craft. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a text about the highest things include a rule about which wood a ladle is made of?
reflect.deeper: The commentators read the rule either as standing for all rites or as praise of the god in fire. What does each reading assume about why a text includes rules?
reflect.practice: Choose one small tool you use daily and give it a moment’s care before you use it.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this rule as his anuvāka 19 and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara as his anuvāka 19; the concordance maps both correctly here.

flags.note: That the rule stands for all Vedic rites as means to release is the anonymous commentator’s and Sāyaṇa’s reading; the text itself states only the rule and its result.
